html:
In the early 1900s São Tomé and Príncipe was among the largest cocoa producers in the world, grown on great estates called roças by contract workers who were in practice slaves.

Cocoa had come from Brazil in the 19th century. After Portugal ended slavery, planters brought labourers called serviçais from Angola on contracts they could not leave, and few ever went home. The British journalist Henry Nevinson exposed the trade in 1906, and Cadbury and other chocolate makers stopped buying São Tomé cocoa in 1909.

The roças, with their great houses, hospitals and railways, still dominate the islands' landscape. Disputes over forced labour later led to the Batepá massacre of 1953.
sum: In the early 1900s São Tomé and Príncipe was among the largest cocoa producers in the world, grown on great estates called roças by contract workers who were in practice slaves.
